lesson.title: Merging Data with update()
lesson.summary: The update() method copies key value pairs from another dictionary or from keyword arguments into an existing dictionary, overwriting any keys that already exist.
lesson.body:
Adding a single new key to a dictionary is easy: dictionary[key] = value. But what if you have a whole second dictionary's worth of new or changed entries and want to fold all of them in at once, without writing a loop yourself? That is the job of the update() method. Calling dictionary.update(other) copies every key value pair from other into dictionary, modifying dictionary in place.

base = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
extra = {"b": 20, "c": 3}
base.update(extra)
print(base)

This prints {'a': 1, 'b': 20, 'c': 3}. The key "a" was untouched because extra had nothing to say about it. The key "b" existed in both dictionaries, and update() resolves that collision by letting the incoming dictionary win, so base's old value of 2 is overwritten by extra's 20. The key "c" did not exist in base at all, so it is simply added. This overwrite-on-collision behavior is the single most important thing to remember about update(): it never merges two conflicting values together, it always just replaces the old one.

update() also accepts keyword arguments directly, which is convenient when you are adding a few known keys without building a separate dictionary first.

base.update(d=4, e=5)
print(base)

This prints {'a': 1, 'b': 20, 'c': 3, 'd': 4, 'e': 5}. Each keyword argument becomes a new key in base, added on top of everything already there.

One detail worth remembering: update() always returns None, because its purpose is to change the dictionary in place, not to hand back a new one. Writing base = base.update(extra) is a common beginner mistake that quietly replaces base with None. If you need a new dictionary instead of modifying an existing one in place, that is exactly what the merge techniques in the next chapter are for.
